chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated from his father, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, who said:

I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the year 255 AH: O my Master! Our companions are divided regarding Divine Unity (Tawhid); some of them say that He is a body, and some of them say that He is an image. If you deem it appropriate, O my Master, to teach me that which I can rely upon and not pass over, I will do so, extending my letter to your servant. Hence, he (peace be upon him) wrote in his own handwriting: You asked about Divine Unity, and this is far from your reach. Allah, the Exalted, is One, Alone, the Eternal Refuge, He begets not nor is He begotten, and none is equal to Him. He is the Creator and not created. He, the Blessed and Exalted, creates whatever He wishes from bodies and other than that, and fashions whatever He wishes, but He is not a fashioned image. Exalted is His Praise, and Hallowed are His Names, and He is High above having a resemblance. He is He, not other than Him. Nothing whatsoever is like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

key_terms.لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ: He begets not, nor is He begotten

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia view on whether God has a body or image according to Imam al-Askari?
ai.summary: In this foundational hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid*, Imam al-Hasan al-Askari (AS) clarifies the Shia doctrine of Divine Unity by distinguishing between Allah as the Creator of bodies and images versus being a body or image Himself. This response addresses the theological confusion of the time by affirming that while Allah creates all forms, He transcends them entirely, rejecting anthropomorphism (*tashbih*) and ensuring His essence remains incomparable. The Imam’s concise reply underscores the principle that Divine Unity is not merely a numerical oneness but an absolute uniqueness that excludes any likeness or physical attribute.
